h1: Dry hopping a homebrew without oxidising it
title: Dry Hopping Without Oxidising Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: When to add dry hops, how to keep oxygen out of the fermenter and how long to leave hops in so hoppy homebrew stays bright.
teaser: Dry hopping is where many hoppy homebrews pick up the oxygen that ruins them. It is avoidable.
standfirst: Dry hops add the aroma that makes a pale ale or IPA worth drinking. Every time you open the fermenter to add them, you also invite in oxygen. Here is how to get the aroma without the stale, dull beer that oxygen leaves behind.
sections: Oxygen is the enemy once fermentation slows

Before and during the first day of fermentation, yeast needs oxygen. After that, oxygen only does damage. It reacts with hop compounds and malt polyphenols, dulling the fresh citrus and tropical aroma within days. Hoppy beers then go darker and pick up flavours of honey, cardboard or dried fruit. Pale, heavily hopped beers show it fastest because there is no roast or caramel character to hide behind.

Dry hopping is risky because it means opening the fermenter late, when the yeast is no longer using up oxygen fast. Pour pellets through an open lid and the air above the beer gets mixed in. Hop pellets also carry a little air of their own.
Add the hops while the yeast can still clean up

The simplest defence is timing. Add dry hops near the end of active fermentation, when the gravity is a few points above its finish and the krausen is starting to fall. Active yeast takes up much of the oxygen you introduce. A small burst of carbon dioxide from the remaining fermentation also helps push air out of the headspace.

Dry hops added at this point can trigger hop creep: enzymes in the hops break down some dextrins and the yeast ferments them, dropping the gravity another point or two. Wait until the gravity is stable for two or three days after dry hopping before you package. Bottling too early is how dry hopped beers become gushers.
Open the fermenter as little as you can

• Have everything ready. Weigh the hops, sanitise the bag or funnel and work fast. The lid should be off for seconds, not minutes.
  • Avoid hop bags you have to fish out. Loose pellets drop to the bottom and settle with the yeast. A bag means opening the lid again to remove it.
  • Do not stir. Pellets break up and disperse on their own.
  • Use a port if your fermenter has one. Some stainless and plastic fermenters have a wide port so you can add hops without lifting the whole lid.

If you have a CO2 cylinder, a quick gentle flush of the headspace after adding the hops helps. Lay the gas over the beer slowly; a strong jet will stir in the air you are trying to remove.
How much hop and for how long

Typical homebrew dry hop rates run from about 2 to 4 g per litre for a pale ale up to 8 g per litre or more for a hazy IPA. For a 20 litre batch, 50 to 100 g is a reasonable range for most hoppy beers. More is not always better. Very heavy rates can bring grassy, vegetal flavours and more beer lost to the hop sludge.

Three to five days of contact at fermentation temperature extracts most of the aroma. Leaving hops in for two weeks gains little and risks grassy flavours. The aroma oils are volatile, so they do not need long.
Packaging is the second danger point

Careful dry hopping counts for nothing if you then splash the beer into a bucket for bottling. Rack gently with the tube outlet below the surface. Bottle or keg as soon as the beer is ready rather than letting it sit. For hoppy beers a keg you can purge with carbon dioxide is far kinder than a bottling bucket. Bottle-conditioned beers do get one help: the yeast in each bottle eats some of the oxygen during conditioning.

When you pour, our guide to pouring bottle-conditioned homebrew keeps the yeast out of your glass. If you plan to keg, kegging homebrew explains purging and closed filling.

Oxidation is a chemical reaction. Like most reactions it runs faster when warm. A hoppy beer stored at 30 °C in an Indian summer will fade far faster than one kept in a fridge. Drink hoppy beers fresh and cold, ideally within a few weeks of packaging.

Working out where oxygen enters your own process is a skill. Most first IPAs taste fine at bottling and dull two weeks later. That gap is what a structured course on cold side process is for.

Your first step: on your next hoppy batch, weigh the dry hops before you open the fermenter. Add them in one go when the gravity is within three or four points of its expected finish.
faqs: When is the best time to dry hop homebrew?
Near the end of active fermentation, when the gravity is a few points above its expected finish. The yeast can still take up some of the oxygen introduced.
How long should dry hops stay in the beer?
Three to five days at fermentation temperature extracts most of the aroma. Much longer can add grassy flavours without more aroma.
Why did my IPA turn dark and dull?
Oxygen picked up after fermentation, often during dry hopping or bottling, is the usual cause. Warm storage makes it happen faster.
